item.title: GOOGLE BIGQUERY: Increasing Google Big Query Daily Query Quota
item.description: How to Raise Google Big Query Daily Query Quota Summary Running batch processes in Google Big Query can hit the daily query quota limit of 20,000. Although, the query-per-day limit is generally raised by Big Query support to prevent abuse scenarios like using it as a calculator. The ceiling can be raised by contacting Google Cloud Support and providing the project ID. Why is the Daily Query Quota Limit Set? item.title: GOOGLE BIGQUERY: Fixing 'Output Field Used as Input' Error

item.title: GOOGLE BIGQUERY: BigQuery's Strange Error
item.description: Why does BigQuery sometimes give a “TABLE_QUERY expressions cannot query BigQuery tables” error? If you use BigQuery, you might have encountered an error message that reads “TABLE_QUERY expressions cannot query BigQuery tables”. This usually happens when you use TABLE_QUERY expressions to query table data instead of metadata. But why does this error occur? The Reason Behind the Error The error message occurs because TABLE_QUERY filters are designed to query only metadata, not table data.

Example of Unexpected Results: SELECT NTH(3, SPLIT(values, ",")) FROM (SELECT "a,b,,d,e" as values) This query returns “d”, whereas one would expect it to return NULL since the third value in the array should be empty.

item.title: GOOGLE BIGQUERY: Understanding REPARTITION in BigQuery Execution Plan

item.title: GOOGLE BIGQUERY: Using SELECT INTO in BigQuery
item.description: How to use SELECT INTO with BigQuery Summary In MySQL, Oracle and Teradata, the SELECT ... INTO FROM ... statement is used to retrieve values from a table and assign them to variables. BigQuery, on the other hand, uses a SET statement to assign values from a subquery to variables. Syntax The syntax for the SET statement in BigQuery is as follows: SET (variable1, variable2, variable3) = (SELECT AS STRUCT column1, column2, column3 FROM table_name WHERE condition LIMIT 1) Here, we assign the values of column1, column2, and column3 to variable1, variable2, and variable3, respectively, from a table called table_name where a certain condition is met.

item.title: GOOGLE BIGQUERY: Logging Different Event Types with Varying Properties on BigQuery
item.description: How to Handle Diversity of Event Types in BigQuery? When logging events from a client component and analyzing them in Google’s BigQuery, a common issue is that the events are of various types with different properties. Solution A general solution with a User-Defined Function (UDF) that can be called for any array type is as follows: CREATE TEMP FUNCTION TopN(arr ANY TYPE, n INT64) AS ( ARRAY(SELECT x FROM UNNEST(arr) AS x WITH OFFSET off WHERE off < n ORDER BY off) ); WITH data AS ( SELECT 1001 as id, ['a', 'b', 'c'] as array_1 UNION ALL SELECT 1002 as id, ['d', 'e', 'f', 'g'] as array_1 UNION ALL SELECT 1003 as id, ['h', 'i'] as array_1 ) SELECT *, TopN(array_1, 2) AS my_result FROM data The above code first defines a UDF called TopN that takes two inputs - an array and a number, and returns the first N elements of the array while keeping the array data type.

item.title: GOOGLE BIGQUERY: Round Timestamp to Nearest 15 Minute Intervals in BigQuery
item.description: Question: How can I round a timestamp to the nearest 15-minute interval using BigQuery standard SQL? Solution: To round a timestamp to the nearest 15-minute interval in BigQuery standard SQL, you can use the following formula: TIMESTAMP_SECONDS(900 * DIV(UNIX_SECONDS(dt_from) + 450, 900)) This formula works by converting the timestamp to Unix time (the number of seconds since January 1, 1970), adding 450 seconds (7.5 minutes) to it, dividing the result by 900 (the number of seconds in 15 minutes), rounding down to the nearest integer, and then multiplying by 900 to get the Unix time of the nearest 15-minute interval.
